text.p: Some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Stockholm's local government must step in to save the city's post offices from being closed down for financial reasons, according to the city's head of real estate. At one post office in Stockholm, retired people now work as volunteers, thus saving the post office from closure.

- Elderly care cannot take more budget cutbacks and streamlining, according to professor Mats Thorslund at a univerity in Stockholm. He says in order to keep care at the current standard it needs more money.

- At 1,200 Swedish companies, the union for electricians is fighting new labour market legislation that allows companies to hire temporary staff. The electricians' employers are talking to other employers about how to handle the conflict. The new labour market legislation, passed by parliament last week, has upset unions and if electricians are succesful, other unions will likely follow suit.

- Almost half of 16 year-old students in three Stockholm schools have problems with spelling, tests show. Of the 800 students taking the tests, half have poor reading comprehension ability and more than a fourth need additional support.
- Power company Stockholm Energi has already prepared for privatisation if the conservative opposition wins general elections in 1998, but no one within the company dares to say this aloud.

- Financial markets expect the Riksbank, or central bank, to cut its key repurchase rate -- which currently stands at 4.35 percent -- on Tuesday when it presents its inflation report. And even when economic trends start picking up sometime next year, the Riksbank is not likely to raise the repo rate by several percentage points. In 1997, the repo rate could be hover around the bottom it is expected to reach early next year.

- Ikano, the private company of the family which created furniture retailer IKEA, will build factory outlet stores with construction giant Skanska. In total, Ikano and Skanska will invest 1.5-2 billion crowns, newspaper sources say.

- U.S. fund Fidelity Investments will soon have 10 percent in Swedish automotive group AB Volvo. While Swedish funds sell Volvo shares, their U.S. counterparts buy. Fidelity has moved in 1996 from holding no Volvo shares to becoming Volvo's largest shareholder by far.

- Swedish funds have received 14 billion crowns to manage thus far in the year, almost double of what they got all of last year. The addition will give the funds an increase in income of at least 100 million crowns more than last year.
